PTM site occupancy and PTM-QTL: occupancy, pairs and trait effects, by mzLib

Source: vignettes/ptmqtl.Rmd
ptmqtl.Rmd

A modification site is rarely all-or-nothing. In one run 15% of a serine is phosphorylated, in the next 40%. That fraction, the site’s occupancy, is what changes with age, dose or genotype, and what two sites can share. Measuring it from label-free data is easy to get wrong: a modified form that was identified but not quantified is not a zero, a site seen only in its modified form is not truly 100%, and two sites read off one peptide are correlated by construction. mzLib’s Quantification.PtmQtl engine keeps those cases apart.

question function mzLib method
what fraction of each site carries its modification, run by run? ptmqtl_occupancy() SiteOccupancyCalculator.Calculate (#1369) intensity occupancy, as MetaMorpheus’s IntensityOccupancy_
the same, for a sample measured as several fractions? ptmqtl_occupancy(samples = ) SiteOccupancyCalculator.Calculate with a run-to-sample map fractions summed before the ratio
which two modifications sit on one molecule? ptmqtl_pairs(type = "physical") PtmPairEngine.Physical (#1430) median co-occupancy
which two sites rise and fall together across runs? ptmqtl_pairs(type = "covarying") PtmPairEngine.CoVarying (#1430, #1446) Spearman’s rho, Benjamini-Hochberg
the same, with runs a site was seen in only one form, or given each run’s depth? ptmqtl_pairs(include_bounds = , run_covariate = ) PtmPairEngine.CoVarying (#1468) tied ranks; partial Spearman
does a site’s occupancy change with a per-run trait? ptmqtl_trait_effects() SiteTraitEffects.Fit (#1446) a mixed model per site, a random intercept per replicate
the same effect in log2 odds, where +1 doubles the odds? ptmqtl_trait_effects(scale = "log2_odds") SiteTraitEffects.Fit (#1464) the natural-log fit over ln 2

Every number below comes from mzLib’s own hand-computed test cases, so each is one mzLib’s tests assert.

The input: one row per peptidoform, per run, per protein

Every function reads a tab-separated table with a header row, mzLib’s own PeptidoformObservation as columns: run; full_sequence in MetaMorpheus notation (PEPS[Common Biological:Phosphorylation on S]K); protein_accession; start_residue and end_residue, the peptide’s first and last residue in that protein, counting from 1; intensity, its MS/MS-quantified intensity in that run, blank when it was identified but not quantified; and optionally previous_residue, the protein residue before the peptide. Four rules decide whether the numbers mean anything:

  • One row per (run, peptidoform, protein), never one per PSM. Two rows for one peptidoform in one run would count its intensity twice; mzLib refuses them.
  • MS/MS identifications only. A match-between-runs transfer is not an identification.
  • Blank, not 0, for “identified but not quantified”. FlashLFQ writes 0 for a peptide it did not quantify. Blank those cells.
  • A shared peptide is one row per protein. Each protein then gets its full intensity. MetaMorpheus instead splits a shared peptide across protein groups, so its IntensityOccupancy_ columns can differ.

mzLib does not build this table for you yet. It has no reader that turns a MetaMorpheus or FlashLFQ result into these rows, because that step makes choices: which PSMs count, how a shared peptide is placed. mzLibR will not make them on mzLib’s behalf. You can assemble the table from two files mzLibR already reads, the PSMs (for runs, proteins and positions) and the FlashLFQ peptide table (for intensities). One way, with your own choices marked:

# Not run: needs your MetaMorpheus search output.
psms <- readers_read_records("AllPSMs.psmtsv")$records
peptides <- readers_read_quantified_peptides("AllQuantifiedPeptides.tsv")$records

# Intensity per (run, full sequence), MS/MS-detected only. FlashLFQ's 0 means "not quantified".
msms <- peptides[peptides$detection_type == "MSMS" & !is.na(peptides$intensity) & peptides$intensity > 0, ]
intensity <- setNames(msms$intensity, paste(msms$sample_label, msms$sequence, sep = "\r"))

# MetaMorpheus writes one value when every protein shares it, else one per protein.
per_protein <- function(cell, count) {
  parts <- strsplit(cell, "|", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  if (length(parts) == 1L) rep(parts, count) else parts
}

# Your choice of PSMs: targets, q-value below 1%, one unambiguous peptidoform.
kept <- psms[psms$decoy_contam_target == "T" & psms$q_value < 0.01 & psms$ambiguity_level == "1", ]
rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(kept)), function(i) {
  p <- kept[i, ]
  accessions <- strsplit(p$protein_accession, "|", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  spans <- per_protein(p$start_and_end_residues_in_parent_sequence, length(accessions))  # "[69 to 84]"
  before <- per_protein(p$previous_residue, length(accessions))
  ends <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(gsub("[][]", "", spans), " to ", fixed = TRUE))
  data.frame(run = p$file_name_without_extension, full_sequence = p$full_sequence,
             protein_accession = accessions, start_residue = as.integer(ends[, 1]),
             end_residue = as.integer(ends[, 2]), previous_residue = ifelse(nchar(before) == 1, before, ""))
}))
rows <- unique(rows)
rows$intensity <- unname(intensity[paste(rows$run, rows$full_sequence, sep = "\r")])
write.table(rows[, c("run", "full_sequence", "protein_accession", "start_residue", "end_residue",
                     "intensity", "previous_residue")],
            "observations.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, na = "")

unique() keeps one row per (run, peptidoform, protein) however many PSMs the peptidoform has, and na = "" writes a blank intensity for a peptidoform that was identified but not quantified. Check that the run names of the two files match: FlashLFQ labels a calibrated file <run>-calib.

Occupancy, run by run

The cases file holds several of mzLib’s hand-computed cases, each on its own protein, named for what it tests:

ptmqtl_data <- system.file("extdata", "ptmqtl", package = "mzLibR")
occ <- ptmqtl_occupancy(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "cases.tsv"))
occ
#> <mzlibr_site_occupancy> 9 sites in 6 runs, 14 cells
#>   quantified 9, floor 1, count_only 3, not_detected 1
r <- occ$records
r[r$protein_accession == "RATIO", c("site_key", "position", "fraction", "unmodified_quantified")]
#>                                           site_key position fraction
#> 3 RATIO:S13:Common Biological:Phosphorylation on S       13     0.15
#>   unmodified_quantified
#> 3                  TRUE

RATIO has 30 units of the phosphopeptide, 70 of the same peptide unmodified, and 100 of a missed-cleavage peptide that also covers the serine: 30 / 200 = 0.15. Every quantified form that covers the position counts in the denominator, whatever its own sequence.

Each cell has a state. Only a "quantified" cell has a fraction:

r[r$protein_accession == "STATES", c("run", "state", "fraction")]
#>           run        state fraction
#> 6   countOnly   count_only       NA
#> 7       floor        floor       NA
#> 8 notDetected not_detected       NA
#> 9       quant   quantified      0.1
state what was seen read it as
quantified the modified form was quantified a measured fraction
floor the modified form was identified but not quantified, while forms covering the site were low, not zero
count_only the modified form was identified, but nothing covering the site was quantified present, amount unknown
not_detected forms covering the site were identified (quantified or not), and none carried the modification a bound below detection, not zero

So never average fraction with the NAs read as 0: they are censored, not absent. Each cell also counts the peptidoforms behind it, identifications rather than intensity: of the covering_peptidoforms identified there, modified_peptidoforms carried the modification.

r[r$protein_accession == "STATES", c("run", "state", "covering_peptidoforms", "modified_peptidoforms")]
#>           run        state covering_peptidoforms modified_peptidoforms
#> 6   countOnly   count_only                     1                     1
#> 7       floor        floor                     2                     1
#> 8 notDetected not_detected                     1                     0
#> 9       quant   quantified                     2                     1

A 1 can be a ceiling. When a site is seen only in its modified form, every quantified form covering it carries the modification, so the fraction is 1. The unmodified form may be there below detection. unmodified_quantified is FALSE then:

r[r$protein_accession == "CEILING", c("fraction", "unmodified_quantified")]
#>   fraction unmodified_quantified
#> 1        1                 FALSE
r[r$protein_accession == "SHARED_POSITION", c("modification", "fraction")]
#>                             modification fraction
#> 4          Common Biological:HexNAc on S      0.3
#> 5 Common Biological:Phosphorylation on S      0.2

Two modifications at one position share a denominator: on SHARED_POSITION, 20 units carry phosphorylation, 30 HexNAc and 50 neither. Positions count from 1, in the protein: a protein N-terminal modification sits at the residue it is on, residue 2 when the initiator methionine was removed. readers_read_occupancy() reads MetaMorpheus’s occupancy file, which puts the N-terminus at position 0, so do not join the two tables on position.

What mzLib leaves out. The cases file also holds rows that make no site: oxidation and carbamidomethylation (mzLib always skips the Common Variable and Common Fixed categories), a peptide N-terminal modification, and N-acetylation on a peptide starting at residue 2 after a K. C-terminal modifications are never sites, because the table does not carry the protein’s length. To keep only some modifications, pass modifications (exact names) or categories (for example "Common Biological").

A sample measured as several fractions

Fractions of one sample are summed before the ratio, as FlashLFQ sums them. Give the run-to-sample map as a file:

fractions <- ptmqtl_occupancy(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "fractions.tsv"),
                              samples = file.path(ptmqtl_data, "fractions_samples.tsv"))
c(runs = fractions$run_count, samples = fractions$sample_count)
#>    runs samples 
#>       3       2
fractions$records[, c("protein_accession", "run", "state", "fraction")]
#>   protein_accession run        state fraction
#> 1      FLOOR_ACROSS   A        floor       NA
#> 2            SUMMED   A   quantified      0.2
#> 3            SUMMED   B not_detected       NA

SUMMED reads 0.3 in fraction 1 and 0.1 in fraction 2. Sample A is (30 + 10) / (100 + 100) = 0.2, not the mean of 0.3 and 0.1. On FLOOR_ACROSS the phosphopeptide was identified, unquantified, in one fraction, and the site was covered in the other: a floor for the sample. Map only fractions together. Technical replicates are separate measurements of one sample; give each its own name, and let ptmqtl_trait_effects() treat them as replicates of one biological sample.

Pairs of modifications

A peptidoform carrying two modifications is direct evidence that both sit on one molecule:

physical <- ptmqtl_pairs(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "cases.tsv"), type = "physical")
physical$records[, c("site_a", "site_b", "statistic", "n", "statistic_n", "p_value")]
#>                                              site_a
#> 1 TWO_ON_ONE:K14:Common Biological:Acetylation on K
#>                                                  site_b statistic n statistic_n
#> 1 TWO_ON_ONE:S13:Common Biological:Phosphorylation on S      0.25 2           1
#>   p_value
#> 1      NA

n is the runs where the doubly modified form was identified (2). statistic is the median co-occupancy over the runs where it was quantified (1): 25 of the 100 units covering both positions carried both marks. There is no test for physical pairs, so p_value and q are NA.

Two sites that rise and fall together across runs are co-varying. mzLib correlates their occupancies with Spearman’s rho, on the runs where both were quantified, and adjusts the p-values with Benjamini-Hochberg within each family. type is required: mzLib has no default between its two methods.

batch <- file.path(ptmqtl_data, "batch.tsv")
plain <- ptmqtl_pairs(batch, type = "covarying")
str(plain[c("covarying_run_count", "min_quantified_fraction", "exclude_ceiling")])
#> List of 3
#>  $ covarying_run_count    : num 12
#>  $ min_quantified_fraction: num 0.7
#>  $ exclude_ceiling        : logi NA
pair_of <- function(result) {
  r <- result$records
  r[startsWith(r$site_a, "PAIR_S") & startsWith(r$site_b, "PAIR_T"), c("statistic", "p_value", "q", "fdr_family", "n")]
}
pair_of(plain)
#>    statistic     p_value           q fdr_family  n
#> 15 0.7622378 0.003950449 0.003950449    A:inter 12

0.7 is mzLib’s default, reported because you did not set it: a site enters pairs only if it is quantified in at least 70% of the runs. exclude_ceiling is NA because you did not choose: mzLib decides it inside PtmPairEngine.CoVarying, and leaves ceilings out. It is FALSE with keep_ceiling = TRUE.

A co-varying pair that was not tested says why in test_status ("not_estimable", "too_few_shared_runs" or "both_sites_mostly_bounds"; "tested" otherwise, NA for physical pairs). run_level_removed says whether rho is partial given the run level; bounds_included and run_covariate_removed say whether one-form runs entered as tied bounds and whether rho is partial given a run covariate, the two options below (mzLib #1468); here they are FALSE.

The trap: a batch correlates everything. These twelve runs come in two batches, and every site reads 0.2 higher in the second. That alone gives PAIR_S and PAIR_T a high rho, though within a batch they are nearly unrelated. remove_run_level = TRUE correlates the two sites given each run’s level, the median occupancy of the other sites in that run:

given <- ptmqtl_pairs(batch, type = "covarying", remove_run_level = TRUE)
pair_of(given)
#>     statistic  p_value        q fdr_family  n
#> 15 0.02857143 0.933543 0.933543    A:inter 12
c(given$run_level_group, given$min_runs_for_run_level, given$min_sites_for_run_level)
#> [1] "none" "10"   "3"

Given the batch, the pair is unrelated. A pair is tested this way only when it shares at least min_runs_for_run_level runs that have a level, and a run has one only with at least min_sites_for_run_level other sites there. Remove the run level for a batch or loading shift only: if the level follows your design - one condition reads higher everywhere - removing it removes the effect you are studying. Sites of different chemistry can have different batch shifts: run_level_group = "category" or "modification" gives each group its own level, and a two-column file (modification, group) as run_level_groups gives any other grouping.

  • overlapping pairs have no q. When one peptide covers both sites, their occupancies share intensities and are correlated by construction, so mzLib reports them but leaves them out of the adjustment.
  • fdr_family is the type (P physical, A co-varying) and whether the two sites are on one protein (intra) or two (inter). q is adjusted within it. It is not a target-decoy q-value.
  • keep_ceiling = TRUE keeps runs where a site was seen only modified. Two unrelated sites that both read 1 in low-load runs then correlate through detection alone; that is why mzLib leaves them out by default.

Counting one-form runs as bounds

A site seen in only one form in a run has no fraction, but it is not missing either. A "not_detected" cell says the occupancy was below what the run could see; a ceiling says it was at the top. By default mzLib leaves such runs out of the correlation. A site that is often below detection then never reaches the 70% guard, and its pairs are never tested.

include_bounds = TRUE lets those runs in as tied ranks, never as invented values (mzLib #1468). A "not_detected" or "floor" cell ties below every fraction of its site. A ceiling, or a "count_only" cell whose covering peptidoforms all carry the mark (k of n with k = n), ties above. A "count_only" cell where both forms were identified has no rank and stays out.

The example is mzLib’s BoundsEnterTypeAAsTiedRanks: two sites with a value in six of ten runs, and a bound in the other four.

bounds <- file.path(ptmqtl_data, "bounds.tsv")
unbounded <- ptmqtl_pairs(bounds, type = "covarying")
str(unbounded[c("row_count", "include_bounds")])
#> List of 2
#>  $ row_count     : num 0
#>  $ include_bounds: logi FALSE
bounded <- ptmqtl_pairs(bounds, type = "covarying", include_bounds = TRUE)
bounded$records[, c("n", "test_status", "bounds_included", "statistic")]
#>   n test_status bounds_included   statistic
#> 1 9      tested            TRUE 0.004201681
str(bounded[c("min_untied_share", "exclude_ceiling")])
#> List of 2
#>  $ min_untied_share: num 0.5
#>  $ exclude_ceiling : logi NA

Six of ten is below the guard, so the plain call tests nothing. With bounds, BOUND_S has a value or a bound in all ten runs and BOUND_T in nine, and the pair is tested on the nine they share. The tenth is BOUND_T’s "count_only" cell with both forms identified (1 of 2): it has no rank. The two sites turn out unrelated (rho 0.004).

Too many ties make the test unreliable. When both sites are mostly one bound, Spearman’s t test calls far too many pairs: in mzLib’s simulation, 2 to 5 times the nominal rate at p < 0.001 with no relation at all. So a pair is tested only if one of its sites has at least min_untied_share (half) of the shared runs outside its largest tie. Otherwise its test_status is "both_sites_mostly_bounds", and it has no p-value.

exclude_ceiling stays NA: with bounds, mzLib treats a ceiling as a high bound. keep_ceiling = TRUE sends FALSE and gives the same answer.

Given each run’s depth

Shallow runs miss low-abundance forms everywhere at once. With bounds in, that makes covered-zeros co-occur across unrelated sites, and any site that rises with depth correlates with every other. run_covariate takes a per-run value, such as the run’s target PSMs, and correlates the two sites given it: a partial Spearman correlation, as for the run level (mzLib #1468).

The file has a header row whose second field names the covariate, then one row per run:

head(read.delim(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "depth_psms.tsv")), 2)
#>   run target_psms
#> 1 r00        9000
#> 2 r01       12000

The example is mzLib’s ARunCovariateIsPartialledOut: twelve runs in two batches, and two sites that also rise a little with each run’s depth.

depth <- file.path(ptmqtl_data, "depth.tsv")
psms <- file.path(ptmqtl_data, "depth_psms.tsv")
depth_pair <- function(result) {
  r <- result$records
  r <- r[startsWith(r$site_a, "DEPTH_S") & startsWith(r$site_b, "DEPTH_T"), ]
  data.frame(rho = round(r$statistic, 2), p = round(r$p_value, 3), n = r$n)
}
depth_pair(ptmqtl_pairs(depth, type = "covarying"))
#>    rho     p  n
#> 1 0.77 0.003 12
covariate <- ptmqtl_pairs(depth, type = "covarying", run_covariate = psms)
depth_pair(covariate)
#>    rho     p  n
#> 1 0.76 0.006 12
str(covariate[c("run_covariate_name", "run_covariate_runs_missing", "min_runs_for_run_level")])
#> List of 3
#>  $ run_covariate_name        : chr "target_psms"
#>  $ run_covariate_runs_missing: chr(0) 
#>  $ min_runs_for_run_level    : num 10
depth_pair(ptmqtl_pairs(depth, type = "covarying", run_covariate = psms, remove_run_level = TRUE))
#>    rho     p  n
#> 1 0.08 0.832 12

Depth alone barely moves rho: in these runs most of the shared rise is the batch. Given the batch’s run level as well, the pair is unrelated. A covariate removes only what it explains.

  • Any increasing transform gives the same answer. The covariate is ranked, so target PSMs and log2 target PSMs are the same input.
  • Leave a run out for “unknown”. It is then left out of every pair, and listed in run_covariate_runs_missing. A blank or NA value is not “unknown”: mzLib refuses it, and mzLibR raises an mzlib_usage_error.
  • The same floor of shared runs applies. A pair partial on the covariate is tested only on at least min_runs_for_run_level shared runs; below that it is "too_few_shared_runs".

Does occupancy change with a trait?

ptmqtl_trait_effects() fits, for each site, logit(occupancy) against a per-run trait, with a random intercept for each biological replicate, so repeated injections of one animal or donor are not counted as independent evidence. The example is mzLib’s TraitDesign: six replicates at three doses, two injections each, built so that logit(occupancy) = -2 + 0.5 x dose + a replicate offset. First compute occupancy, and write it to a file:

written <- ptmqtl_occupancy(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait.tsv"),
                            out = file.path(tempdir(), "trait_occupancy.tsv"))
c(cells_written = written$written$row_count, rows_returned = nrow(written$records))
#> cells_written rows_returned 
#>            24             0
written$state_counts
#>   quantified        floor   count_only not_detected 
#>           23            1            0            0
head(read.delim(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_runs.tsv")), 3)
#>    run replicate dose injection
#> 1 R0_0        R0 0.25         1
#> 2 R0_1        R0 0.25         0
#> 3 R1_0        R1 0.25         1

The runs table gives each run its replicate, then the trait, then any covariates, each column named by its header. Then fit (here on the file the call above writes, as this package ships it):

effects <- ptmqtl_trait_effects(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_occupancy.tsv"),
                                file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_runs.tsv"))
effects
#> <mzlibr_trait_effects> 2 sites against dose, given injection (min 6 runs, 4 replicates), on natural_log_odds
#>   fitted 2, below_support 0, too_few_observations 0, rank_deficient 0, too_few_groups 0, variance_ratio_at_limit 0, not_converged 0
effects$records[, c("protein_accession", "status", "effect", "standard_error", "df", "q", "runs", "replicates")]
#>   protein_accession status    effect standard_error df           q runs
#> 1     CENSORED_SITE fitted 0.5428795     0.06507235  3 0.003610195   10
#> 2        TRAIT_SITE fitted 0.5008514     0.05519014  4 0.001634666   12
#>   replicates
#> 1          5
#> 2          6

TRAIT_SITE recovers the 0.5 it was built with. effect is in logit units per unit of the trait - natural-log odds, mzLib’s default scale, which effects$scale reports - so exp(0.5) = 1.65: each dose unit multiplies the odds of the modified form by about 1.65. The degrees of freedom are between replicates (six replicates, less the intercept and the dose), because the dose never varies within a replicate. CENSORED_SITE is the same site with one replicate’s two runs replaced by a floor and a ceiling. Both leave the fit - only quantified, non-ceiling cells are responses - so it rests on five replicates and three degrees of freedom.

Support. A site needs min_runs runs and min_replicates replicates with a response, mzLib’s defaults reported in the result. Ask for six replicates, and CENSORED_SITE is below support:

strict <- ptmqtl_trait_effects(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_occupancy.tsv"),
                               file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_runs.tsv"), min_replicates = 6)
strict$records[, c("protein_accession", "status", "effect", "replicates")]
#>   protein_accession        status    effect replicates
#> 1     CENSORED_SITE below_support        NA          5
#> 2        TRAIT_SITE        fitted 0.5008514          6

In log2 odds. Natural-log odds are mzLib’s default. scale = "log2_odds" reports the same fit in log2 odds, where an effect of +1 doubles the odds of the modified form per trait unit (mzLib #1464):

log2 <- ptmqtl_trait_effects(file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_occupancy.tsv"),
                             file.path(ptmqtl_data, "trait_runs.tsv"), scale = "log2_odds")
c(effects$scale, log2$scale)
#> [1] "natural_log_odds" "log2_odds"
data.frame(site = effects$records$protein_accession,
           natural = round(effects$records$effect, 3), log2 = round(log2$records$effect, 3),
           p_natural = signif(effects$records$p_value, 3), p_log2 = signif(log2$records$p_value, 3))
#>            site natural  log2 p_natural   p_log2
#> 1 CENSORED_SITE   0.543 0.783  0.003610 0.003610
#> 2    TRAIT_SITE   0.501 0.723  0.000817 0.000817

TRAIT_SITE’s 0.50 natural-log units are 0.72 log2 units: 2^0.72 = 1.65, the same odds ratio per dose unit. mzLib does not refit. It divides the effects and standard errors by ln 2 and the two variances by (ln 2)^2, so df, p_value and q are unchanged. Pick the scale your other results use; the science does not change.

This answers “does the modified share change?”, not “is the modification detected more often?”: floors, count-only and undetected cells are left out, never entered as 0. q adjusts over this call’s fitted sites only - not across datasets, and not a target-decoy q-value.

What these functions will not do

  • No reader builds the input. mzLib has none yet, so the table above is yours to assemble.
  • No test for physical pairs. mzLib reports their co-occupancy and counts only.
  • No detection model. For “is the modification detected more often?”, fit a logistic model per site with stats_fit_logistic() on a 0/1 table of your own.
  • mzLibR does no arithmetic. Every number on this page came from mzLib.

What to cite

The methods and resources behind the functions on this page, from their specs:

  • doi:10.2307/1412159: the rank correlation coefficient rho of co-varying pairs (Spearman, Am J Psychol 15:72, 1904).
  • doi:10.5351/CSAM.2015.22.6.665: ppcor, whose pcor.test(method = ‘spearman’) the partial correlation given the run level reproduces (Kim, Commun Stat Appl Methods 22:665, 2015).
  • doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x: the step-up adjustment behind q, within each fdr_family (Benjamini and Hochberg, J R Stat Soc B 57:289, 1995).
  • doi:10.2307/2529876: the random-intercept linear mixed model fitted per site (Laird and Ware, Biometrics 38:963, 1982).
